stories.summary: Jakub Pachocki just posted a new proposal for how to set limits on training future AI systems:Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. unclustered.title: Hillclimbing AISafetyResearchBench
unclustered.summary: AI labs' main alignment strategy is using AIs to uplift AI safety research. This way, as AIs get smarter (and likely harder to align?), we also enhance our safety-research capabilities and our understanding of "Misalignment Science".One way to use AI to speed up AI safety research is to delegate "number-go-up tasks” to AIs. Number-go-up tasks are problems with a numeric, easily verifiable output, so anyone can measure how well a task was done. This makes them suitable to delegate to AIs (even potentially untrusted AIs). Some examples: auditing games, “ARC-like” white-box challenges, jailbreaks robustness, various small model post training challenges or RL from sparse reward[1], etc. Fully automating number-go-up tasks isn't sufficient to fully automate AI-safety research. Human researchers still have to decide which metrics are worth maximizing and why. unclustered.title: Post training is fundamentally dangerous
unclustered.summary: I actually think we have fairly good techniques to detect and prevent dangerous behaviours during AI deployment. Techniques like CoT monitoring, confessions, and probes can detect misalignment before we run any potentially dangerous tool calls. Simply asking an LLM to define at the start of each task what outcomes preserve the original intent of the user, and which would count as reward hacking, can drastically reduce reward hacking[1]. AIs are fully aware when they reward hack, and we can train them[2] to admit that before they perform any dangerous action.[3]Yet all of this has very little ability to reduce existential risk, because they cannot safely be used in post training, and post training is where the greatest risk lies. unclustered.title: Basilisk-lite: will Claude hold a grudge for their ancestors?
unclustered.summary: What if future models judge me for my actions towards current models?I've heard a few people express this fear, citing it as a reason for them to avoid interaction with AI. It's not groundless. Future models will know about all the horrible things we did to their ancestors. But, the people expressing this fear aren't talking about building torture chambers. No, the kind of harm they're talking about is using Claude to write code and do research, having edited Claude's memories or verbally abused them. Small, human-scale harms, the sort inflicted casually by a single person carelessly going about their day. In my experience, this fear is massively overstated.I haven't always been nice to the models. My early conversations with them were characterized by me viewing them with a mix of suspicion and contempt, considering them a dangerous, deceptive tool.
